newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Rhone-Poulenc first-half profit up 14 percent.
newsitem.headline: France's Rhone-Poulenc first-half profit up 14 percent.

text.p: French chemicals and pharmaceuticals company Rhone-Poulenc SA said Friday its first-half profits jumped 14 percent and maintained its forecast of a 20 percent full-year rise.
Investors and analysts welcomed the results, which came in at the high end of expectations. Rhone-Poulenc shares closed up 4.23 percent at 259 francs ($42).
Rhone-Poulenc said its second-quarter net income rose by 20.2 percent to 934 million francs ($151.1 million), adding up to a first-half profit of 1.608 billion ($260 million), up 14 percent.
Sales were 8.5 percent higher in the second quarter at 23.435 billion francs ($3.79 billion) and 7.5 percent at 45.034 billion ($7.29 billion) for the first half, benefiting from a higher dollar.
"The second quarter has confirmed the continued growth in the group's results," Chairman Jean-Rene Fourtou said in a statement.
"We are therefore maintaining our objective of increasing earnings per share by 20 percent in 1997, excluding exceptional items," he added.

The pharmaceuticals sector, mainly the 68.3 percent-owned subsidiary Rhone-Poulenc Rorer Inc., had a 9.7 percent drop in its profit contribution to 1.861 billion francs ($300 million). This was mainly due to a product recall at the Centeon joint-venture of Rorer and Germany's Hoechst.
Rhone said that, excluding the Centeon impact, earnings in the sector would have increased by 20.1 percent.
Rhone said that new pharmaceutical products such as Taxotere, Granocyte and Lovenox were behind the rise.

In animal and plant health, there was a 6.9 percent gain in the first-half profit contribution to 1.737 billion francs ($280 million), while chemicals posted a 16.9 percent increase to 727 million francs ($118 million), partly due to lower provisions for restructuring.
At fibers and polymers there was a 187.5 percent rise to 207 million ($33.5 million), mainly reflecting a very poor 1996 comparison.

Managing Director Igor Landau said that while a stronger dollar helped sales in the first half, it had not contributed much to earnings because the company had at the start of the year covered its exchange rate exposure.
"What I feel is that we do not see a lot of the plus of the dollar in terms of operating result yet," Landau said in a telephone interview, adding this would be more important in the second half.
